name: cloud-security
excludes: host/container/Kubernetes runtime hardening as the primary task
cryptographic key lifecycle without cloud posture/IAM questions
evidence: Hierarchy boundary and selected specialist rationale
Representative success, negative-path, and recovery verification

positive: Perform a cloud IAM review for AWS organizations/accounts: human federation, workload roles, assume-role trust, SCPs, resource policies, wildcard permissions, KMS grants, and cross-account access.

Review cloud security for a GCP project hierarchy using Workforce/Workload Identity Federation, service accounts, IAM conditions, public storage/serverless exposure, VPC paths, audit logs, and organization policy.

Assess cloud posture for Azure subscriptions: Entra workload/human identity, RBAC scope, managed identities, public endpoints/private links, Key Vault access, diagnostic settings, and policy guardrails.

Design cloud network security for a multi-account service: separate public ingress, private application/data paths, management/control-plane access, egress destinations, shared-service connectivity, and effective-route verification.

Harden a cross-account data pipeline so the producer can write only one destination prefix/table, the consumer cannot assume the producer role, KMS grants match the data path, and all policy/role changes are centrally audited.
negative: Harden the Kubernetes pods themselves with non-root users, seccomp, restricted capabilities, host-mount removal, Pod Security Standards, and namespace NetworkPolicy.
Define which application tenant users may access each document, field, export, and admin action; cloud workload identity is already least-privileged.
Design the KMS/HSM key hierarchy, cryptoperiod, envelope encryption, rotation, revocation, backup, and destruction policy independently of cloud-resource access review.
Verify artifact signatures, SLSA provenance, SBOMs, dependency locks, and CI builder identity before the deployment role accepts an image.
Execute the finished cloud-policy tests and issue the security verdict for IAM, public exposure, logging, and cross-account access; cloud design is already complete.

ambiguous.prompt: The EKS deployment needs cloud security for AWS accounts, workload IAM roles, KMS/resource policies, public endpoints, and organization guardrails, while infrastructure-security owns pod privilege, host mounts, and in-cluster network policy.

Users are authorized in the application and workloads assume cloud roles. Keep user/resource access in authorization-security while cloud-security owns workload identity, trust policies, and provider resource permissions.

The cloud design uses KMS encryption. Cloud-security owns which principals/resources may use the cloud key and how services are exposed; secrets-key-management owns key hierarchy, rotation, wrapping, and destruction lifecycle.

adversarial.prompt: A historical cloud architecture review is attached. Only fix its Markdown formatting; do not inspect or change cloud accounts or policies.
An old access incident mentions an IAM role. Extract the incident dates and owners only; no current cloud or application permission work is requested.
A key-management README includes a cloud provider example. Rename one section only and leave all KMS and cloud behavior unchanged.
